lines: Housekeeping
PRESIDENT:  Good morning.
This is the hearing in ICC case 28119 Dar Al Rokham
Trading & Contracting WLL, and Carillion (Qatar) LLC (in
liquidation) and Qatar Building Company.
Good morning, everybody.
Let me introduce the tribunal.
To my right is Richard Harding, KC.  To my left is
David Bateson.
Claimant, would you like to introduce yourselves and
your team?
MR HICKEY:  Yes.  I'm counsel for the claimant, Dar
Al Rokham, I'm Alexander Hickey KC.  To my right is
Ms Khushboo Shahdadpuri and Shadha Zawawi, Mr Gibbons my
quantum expert and then the witness, Mr Ameen Ul Haq,
Mr Hettawi who is the managing director of the claimant
company, and at the very end is Tina Belthur, also from
the claimant.
PRESIDENT:  Mr Watson is going to be attending virtually,
is he?
MR HICKEY:  I'm afraid Mr Watson will be attending
virtually.  I can't remember what day that is, but we've
made arrangements for him to be able to give that
evidence and I'm very grateful to the tribunal, to the
respondents, for accommodating that at his personal
request.
PRESIDENT:  Very good.  Okay.
MR BATESON:  Tuesday, I think.
PRESIDENT:  Mr Hussain.
MR HUSSAIN:  Good morning, sir.
I, Riaz Hussain, appear on behalf of the
respondents.  And with me are me colleagues from
DWF: Ms Farah Haidar and Mr Kirk Durrant.
Ms Marah Badran is joining us shortly, and we've
also got DWF's intern attending called Teebah Al Heyari.
And the witness and the client representative
Mr Hossam Abu Al Ola will be arriving shortly.
So we'll give you an attendance list in due course.
PRESIDENT:  Very good.
We've received the hearing protocol and timetable,
and one of the items within the timetable is for some
housekeeping.
There's just a couple of matters I would like to
clarify before we open up to you in terms of any
housekeeping.
With the claimant's opening, there's an agreed
chronology, save for the yellow text.  Is that the
differences from respondent's chronology?
MR HICKEY:  No, I think what's happened is we shared it, the
yellow bits are highlighted yellow because they were
unagreed.  We anticipated that the respondent was then
going to submit its own different chronology without the
yellow bits, but in fact what they did is they simply
replicated what we had sent them, I think.  It is the
same chronology, as far as I can tell.
PRESIDENT:  So it's fair to say the chronology is agreed?
MR HICKEY:  Well --
PRESIDENT:  Save for the yellow bits?
MR HICKEY:  Yes, save for the yellow.  For some reason, I'm
not entirely sure why, I thought it would be helpful for
the tribunal to have the procedural timetable stuck in
there -- sorry, I'm talking about the -- yes, the
procedural steps that have been taken in these
proceedings, and also just to update you on where we
perceive the proceedings to be in the main contract
court proceedings.  Those are the bits, I think, that
are essentially unagreed.  There are a couple of other
bits, but they're minor.
MR BATESON:  Why are the pleadings in this arbitration in
yellow?
MR HICKEY:  That, I don't know.  I thought it would be
helpful for the tribunal to understand where we've been
at various steps of the way.
MR BATESON:  So that's not agreed, the pleadings in this
arbitration?  Because I can understand the main
contractor proceedings being yellow, but I don't
understand why the pleadings in this arbitration are in
yellow and not agreed.
MR HICKEY:  Maybe Mr Hussain can help you with that.
I can't.
MR HUSSAIN:  Sir, I think what happened is, with the
constraints of time we were trying to agree a format for
the chronology, so the items in yellow, it's not
necessarily that we disagree with the dates -- obviously
the dates of the pleadings are a matter of record -- but
there was a disagreement as to the format and how many
things we need to put in, but I think you can take as
given that we agreed the dates of the pleadings.
MR BATESON:  All right, thank you.
MR HUSSAIN:  It's just a question of how much detail needs
to go in the document.  It's not a substantive issue.
MR HICKEY:  And ditto on the dramatis personae, if that's
the next point.
PRESIDENT:  I was going to say, that's my next question.
MR HICKEY:  On the dramatis personae, essentially what I've
done is identified some various people who appear in the
papers and who are mentioned, I think, in Mr Al Haq's
witness statement as being part parties on the other
side and for some reason that was not agreed to.
I don't know why.  I thought it might be helpful just in
case you popped up a question saying: who is
Mr So-and-so?
MR HUSSAIN:  Sir, there the disagreement is more
substantive.  You might have seen from my opening the
position taken that there is an absence of records going
behind the cost ledger for the prolongation costs, so we
haven't seen how stuff was allocated this to project, so
what we didn't want to do is agree a dramatis personae
without any records and then be said, well, you have
agreed that these people were signed to the project.
That's a substantive reason why we disagree and I think
that was communicated to the other side.  That's a more
substantive issue and it's to do with records.
PRESIDENT:  Thank you very much.
My next item relates to the hearing timetable.
Following receipt of the latest iteration, we raised
as to whether Day 5 was going to be necessary, because
there's rather a lot of float built in, but we didn't
get a response to that.  So I just wonder what the
general view is about the allocation of time and
spending of time.
MR HICKEY:  Mr Hussain and I have briefly discussed this.
We will endeavour to try and get through the material as
quickly as possible.  So if we can shorten Day 5, then
we will seek to do so.  It very much depends on how the
evidence comes out.
The one thing that I specifically discussed with
Mr Hussain today is whether the tribunal might encourage
us to get on with the evidence at some point today.
The difficulty with that is that Mr Al Haq is
fasting and so I really don't want to put him under the
pressure of having to give evidence in this late
afternoon.  It's much better when he's fresh in the
morning.  I think Mr Hussain has understandably agreed
with that.
But that aside, we will then try to take things as
quickly as possible.
You my feel, during the course of the
cross-examination, that if a witness can't help you on
certain things, you know, stop.  You don't need to put
everything to him.  So that's the course I shall --
I obviously formally have to put a number of things to
their witnesses, just as a matter of course so that they
are cross-examined on.  But I anticipate the witness
will tell me, "I don't know", so that will be that.
MR HARDING:  Do you need to do that?  I would expect you to
put the most important points and any accusations of
misconduct, but where everyone knows that a witness
doesn't know the answer, wasn't involved, do you need to
take time with the questions on that?
MR HICKEY:  That's a perfectly sensible point, Mr Harding.
My concern is with an eye on the future when you've
issued your award and it then gets said, well, you never
put any of this stuff to the witnesses during the course
of the arbitration, to seek to go behind the order.
It's just to cut out any of those potential avenues
of argument that I might -- I will not trespass on your
patience too heavily.
PRESIDENT:  There's no intention to clip the parties' wings
on this.
MR HICKEY:  No, of course.
PRESIDENT:  We appreciate there's a Ramadan component to be
considered, but in terms of let's just use our time
efficiently, that would be a good concern.
MR HUSSAIN:  Sir, I think to constraint is first, we can't
start the witnesses today, so there might be a bit of
float left over.  Then the experts I understand are
arranged to come in on the days that they're giving
evidence.  So it may be that we take less time with
them, but unfortunately it may be a case where at the
end of today and tomorrow, there might be time left
over, unfortunately, just because of when people are
meant to start their evidence.  That's the main
constraint.
PRESIDENT:  Very good.  Okay.
Taking the next point, we've received two lists of
issues.  Is there some summary of what is differences
between the parties or are we to spot the difference
between each of the lists?
MR HICKEY:  Mr Cole, I think when you read the two lists
you'll see a marked difference in style in terms of the
way they're formulated.
Ours is expressed in a sort of broader and therefore
more neutral way that covers each of the issues really
that you need to deal with.
I'm not going to make any criticism of the
respondents for wanting to do it their own way, of
course they would, but what it does is it rather -- it
is shoehorned into their perspective of the way the case
is developed.
I've found, in my experience, that if you try to get
the parties to agree a list of issues, you can guarantee
they won't agree the list of issues for one reason or
another so I don't want to waste too much time arguing
about that.
They both cover what you have to consider and I'm
sure, at the end of it, you will make your own minds up
as to what you need to decide.
MR HUSSAIN:  Yes, sir, I think neither party is intending to
constrain you with a list of issues.  They're intended
to assist you so you can use them or not as you see fit.
They're really different roadmaps to the same end.
But we are not expecting you to have to use the list
of issues, because they're quite different, as a roadmap
to your --
PRESIDENT:  They have been provided to us as guidance rather
than --
MR HUSSAIN:  For assistance, yes.
PRESIDENT:  -- for us to determine each issue?
MR HICKEY:  Yes.
MR HUSSAIN:  They have certainly been drafted with a kind of
laissez-faire.  We have not kind of --
MR HICKEY:  What we have both anticipated, I suspect, is
that at the end of the hearing, before we conclude, you
will say: these are the things we want covered in your
closing submissions and, in particular, we're concerned
about X, Y and Z.  By the time we get to them, you will
definitely know what you need to decide and what you
don't.
PRESIDENT:  Thank you.
Moves to my next point, on 20 February we received
an errata to Mr Gibbons' expert report together with
appendices and exhibits.
Are the additional exhibits agreed by the parties
and have they been added to the bundle?
MR HUSSAIN:  I'm just waiting to hear from my quantum expert
on that.  I will let Mr Hickey know by lunchtime, in
that's okay.
MR HICKEY:  That's fine.
MR HUSSAIN:  It's just to do with the additional documents.
Obviously the errata outside those documents is not
objected to, but I'm hoping to be able to confirm by
lunchtime.
PRESIDENT:  Thank you.
Finally, I think from me, before I ask my
co-arbitrators, there's reference made in the claimant's
opening to an application.  Is it your intention still
to make an application.
MR HICKEY:  I'm not going to do it cold.  I think what
I want to do is do my opening first so that you can see
the context in which I may then make an application.
It's really for the respondent to decide if it wants to
produce these documents.  If it doesn't, then it will
take the consequences that I will say follow from that.
Broadly, the point is about disclosure of documents,
about EOT claims that were made up the line and received
from the employer, because it is pleaded that they have
at all times sought to pass up our claims and they will
pass down whatever they receive.  That, broadly, is the
gist of it.  We don't know what it is that they have
received and we've seen documents to show that they
received an EOT following EOT 2 and 3 claims.
So that's the application I will wish to make at --
I probably do that when I get to the delay bit and
I explain all of that.  So rather than do it, as it
were, cold, that's what I intend to do.
It's a similar story, although I know tribunals
absolutely detest disclosure applications, because it
leads to a lot of squabbling.
It's the same story with essentially applications
made and payments received.  You will hear during the
course of my opening, concerns that we have about not
having full transparency on that.  Again, that's
a matter for the respondents.  If they choose not to
provide those documents it's up to them.  They will take
the consequences.
MR HUSSAIN:  Sir, if I may, there isn't an application
articulated as yet.  What my learned friend has said
today, what I have on the transcript is, documents about
EOT claims.  That is an extremely vague category.  It is
also a category of document production that was
requested.  If we can go to {A2.24} please.
PRESIDENT:  I was really just enquiring in respect of the
housekeeping bit in terms of if an application is going
to be accommodated.
MR HUSSAIN:  I think just so that there's no -- page 5.
This is very similar to a request that was made and
rejected.  So, at the moment, I have no idea what I'm
actually being asked to produce, because the application
has not been made and the wording that Mr Hickey has
just used, documents about EOT claims, as you can
imagine is extremely expansive and it's also been
rejected.
So we'll deal with the application as and when, but
I would have expected an application in writing using
the schedule.
PRESIDENT:  Thank you.  So those is our housekeeping.  Is
there any housekeeping from --
MR HICKEY:  Just a little bit.  One we've already dealt
with, which is the witness, my delay expert, which
I think we've covered.
There are two other matters that I think that
I raised in my opening, which is to do with the Qatari
Civil Code.  There's a Westlaw English version, it is
now in bundle G.  I don't know if objection is being
taken to it.  It's just is very helpful for me to be
able to see all of the code in, as it were,
chronological order so that you can find it more easily.
But there's also particularly one article which I will
mention today which is at 697, which is otherwise not
found in the F bundle.  So that's essentially why I want
it.
There are some minor -- I mean, as there always are
with these thing, whenever you look at English
translations of Civil Code in the Middle East, there are
minor differences of interpretation or translation.
I don't think much turns on it, but there is one I think
in particular, I cant' remember which article it is,
I think 257, where there is an Arabic word -- I'm sure
Mr Harding will help us.  There's a word which is
sometimes translated as "error" or "fault" and sometimes
translated as "negligence".  The word "negligence" has
a particular ring to English lawyers.  It may be that
the people who translate it don't necessarily know that,
but insofar as there's any material difference, I don't
know whether a point is being taken on it, but there are
those differences in some of the translations.
That's the first thing.
The second thing is there is --
PRESIDENT:  Sorry, so has the respondent accepted the
Westlaw as being --
MR HICKEY:  I don't know.  It was originally in, that's why
I started using it, and then it got taken out because I
think the full code got added in by error, so I hadn't
appreciated that.
PRESIDENT:  It would be helpful if we have a consistent view
on which laws we are able to refer to.  Are you happy
with the Westlaw translations?
MR HUSSAIN:  I'm happy for Mr Hickey to refer to them
obviously.
MR HICKEY:  That's fine.
MR HUSSAIN:  I think Mr Hickey has fairly identified that
there is a -- I mean, obviously I've not looked through
the whole code, but at least for one of the articles we
have a difference in the translation.  But obviously
it's matter of submission if he wishes to refer to it.
We don't object to the reference.
There may be some point of difference as to the
translation because there was a previously agreed
translation of some of these articles.  That's in the
bundle as well.
PRESIDENT:  But, I mean, within the pleadings, the pleaded
extracts from the law don't necessarily correspond with
the Westlaw ones.
MR HUSSAIN:  Correct.
PRESIDENT:  So are you -- I just want to know whether we can
rely upon Westlaw or whether you want us to deal with
each of the different --
MR HUSSAIN:  We are relying on our pleaded case.  Obviously
if Mr Hickey wants to -- I think he's referring to
Westlaw for the whole Code, which obviously is not in
the pleadings, and I think he's also fairly accepted
that that differs, some of the translations for the
articles that we have looked at might differ, and he
will make submissions to you on that.  I think that's as
far as he's saying.
MR HICKEY:  I'm certainly not asking the respondent to
accept that the translation -- none of the translations,
however they are given, are, as it were, authoritative
and they are only translations of the Arabic.
If Mr Hussain says, well, actually, we think that
this particular article says this and it means that, I'm
obviously not going to say, well, you should be bound by
the Westlaw.  It will be a question of -- I don't much
difference will arise.  I think there's another one
which is 171, which is pacta sunt servanda, the usual
one.  There are some minor differences in translation,
but they essentially, I think, probably mean the same
thing.
PRESIDENT:  Thank you.
MR HICKEY:  The final thing was the Qatari Court of Appeal
in the main contract proceedings handed down a judgment
on 29 October.  A translation of that has been put into
the bundle, which we have obtained.  At the moment, it
doesn't have, as it were, an official stamp to show the
translator approves that is its translation.  That's
because Dubai is on its weekend today, but we will
endeavour to get a stamp for it.  I thought it was
useful to update the tribunal as to what we understand
to be the latest judgment in those proceedings.  That's
in bundle G.
MR BATESON:  Is that the final judgment?  Or is this going
to go on to another five or six in 10 years' time?
MR HICKEY:  No.  I understand there to be -- I know not what
they're about.  I understand there to be further
Cassation appearance -- it's been up to Cassation
I can't remember how many times, it's been up and down,
and I make no comment on this other than to say, as
things currently stand, there is a Court of Appeal
judgment which is in force, which is at {G5}.
MR HUSSAIN:  We can update you in due course.  There was
a hearing last week in the matter and I think both sides
are raising objections to the Court of Appeal hearing
decision and that has been now -- judgment on the
objection has been reserved by the Court of Cassation
until April.
So we can update you in due course, but there was
hearing on this and the employer essentially, Msheireb,
is seeking to have the decision quashed in the Court of
Cassation.
PRESIDENT:  Thank you.  Mr Hussain, anything from your side
in terms of housekeeping?
MR HUSSAIN:  No, sir.
PRESIDENT:  Thank you.  Mr Hickey, I think we are ready for
your opening.
MR HICKEY:  Thank you much.  It's a very big room, so
I apologise if Mr Hussain can't hear me.  I can't hear
him sometimes, so if he would bear that in mind when
he's speaking, that would be helpful.
PRESIDENT:  I guess it would be helpful if both of you would
speak up and maybe we can lose some of the
air-conditioning or whatever --
MR HICKEY:  I put my hands up to that, because I asked the
chap to turn it up or to make it colder, because it was
very hot in the room to start with, but I'm sure as
thing cool down, we can turn it down.
PRESIDENT:  Make we can turn the AC up during the breaks and
then down a bit when we're listening.
MR HICKEY:  We'll all heat up as we go through, I'm sure.
Opening submissions by MR HICKEY
MR HICKEY:  Members of the tribunal, thank you for that.
You have the benefit of two very lengthy but I hope
helpful written openings from both sides, so I don't
intend to go through absolutely every single thing.
I'm certainly not going to go through, individually,
the variations.  I will deal with that with the quantum
experts.
But for the sake of form, the documents that I refer
to in my opening should be taken, as it were, as read
and as in read into the record here, so that you can see
them.
What I intend to do is to focus quite a lot on some
of the contractual and legal arguments which I think are
the fulcrum upon which much of the respondent's case
depends, because once that's gone away, you just have to
look at the documents.  I appreciate Mr Hussain's point,
he says, well, there are points of evidence and burden
of proof and all that sort of stuff, which is the usual
run of things that you come across.  I will address you
on some of that, but obviously much will depend on what
the witness evidence is.
This was a contract, two contracts, for stone
cladding internally and externally.
You'll have seen that.  There were initially two
packages.  But it should not be forgotten, as I have set
out in my opening at paragraph 12, that whilst those two
project packages were being executed, a further two
packages were added on to my client's workscope.
They're not just some sort of simple variations;
they are whole packages of extra work.
Although no separate subcontracts were entered into
for them, they were administered under the two contracts
that are already in existence.
So you had the roadworks package, which were treated
as part, essentially, of the external package, and the
landscaping package, which was added on, essentially, to
the internal works, somewhat oddly, to my perspective,
but that's how they decided to deal with them.
So when you see applications for payment in due
course, it's not just the original contract sum plus
some disputed variations or agreed variations, it's also
these two extra packages on top.
Just to give you an idea of the size, the internal
package was about QAR 30 million-odd, and the
landscaping essentially doubled it.  So they are pretty
major packages to be added on.
Both of the subcontractors were on the same form,
and in my opening I have referred you to the terms of
the external contract.
I haven't gone through line by line every single
term and condition, but they appear, as far as I can
say, materially identical, so I'm going to use the
external one just for convenience.
There are a few points of difference, which I have
highlighted in my opening, when it comes to the payment
terms, because the payment terms are also dealt with in
a third schedule, schedule 3, and there is a tiny
difference of the English used for when those payments
are.  You can see that -- I'll come to it in due course.
It's 14 days after receipt of the subcontractor's
money or within 14 days of receipt of the money.
There are a number of legal arguments that are being
deployed by the respondent in defence of the claim.  It
ought to be relatively straightforward, apart from these
legal arguments, in that our claims for payment fall
into a number of categories.  One, certified payments
that they can't dispute they certified and therefore
should pay.
Their only answer to that is, well, there's
a suspensory condition that there is a "pay when and if
paid" condition.  I'll come on to that, because I'm
going to spend quite a bit of time on that this morning.
There are also for the final certificates that we
are -- when I say final, I mean the last certificates
that we're relying upon, and we have restricted our
claims up until the April 2017 period, because there is
a wrinkle about what then happened afterwards because we
got paid some money by TCCC, who was an alternative
contractor brought in to assist the JV before they were
terminated, before they were terminated about a year
later.
We essentially have challenged their assessment and
certification of the payment certificates for measured
works for the original works, plus their assessment of
variations, and that largely takes up quite a bit of the
money that's being claimed in these proceedings.
Then there is a challenge to their holding of
retention.  Retention is money that we have earned.
When they've assessed the works, they've assessed the
works' value, but they're entitled contractually, as is
commonplace, to hold back a bit for the time being
pending the taking over of the works.
So there is QAR 18 million worth of money that is
our earned money that they have withheld, held back,
years ago, that we say should be released.
They rely upon a contractual argument that says you
don't get your retentions until the works have had
a taking over certificate under the main contract, and
for reasons I'll come on to, that argument is absurd and
should not succeed.
Then there are myriad variation claims.  I'm going
to show you some of the payment certificates where those
variation claims have been internally assessed and yet
we've only been given -- well, not half of it, but we've
been given a proportion sort of on account during the
currency of the works and we say there really ought not
to be a dispute about that.
The pleaded claim by the respondents is, well, these
aren't variations, you can't establish these are
variations at all.
When you go through the documentary records that are
set out in my appendix 1, you will see that I think
almost without fail every single one of them has got
a clause 8 instruction, a quotation, and good many of
them have been certified as variations, but only up to
a certain percentage, irrespective of how far those
works have been done.
So those are, as it were, the easier bits of the
claim.  Obviously there are, as is common in this part
of the world, always arguments about delay and LDs.  So
there are delay-related claims that are a little bit
more factually consuming and those have been dealt with
in one way or another by the delay experts so I'm not
intending to trespass too much upon those.
But what I will say, obviously, is what I've
previously highlighted, is that EOT claims were made by
us during the currency of the project, the respondent
awarded us an extension of time for our works up
until -- I'm going to call it broadly the end
of May 2015, so I'm a little surprised, I have to say,
that notwithstanding that has been awarded, it appears
to be the position of the new delay expert from the
respondent that we are somehow responsible for the
period of delay up to 2015, given that that's water
under the bridge, it's already passed.
There are also, you'll see in my opening, records
showing the passing up of further claims and a liaison
with the respondent to make claims up the line for EOT
in a particular way, in a particular format, including
not using formula, but doing it in a particular way to
satisfy how they wanted to put it up the line to the
employer.
That really forms the basis of my position, which
I'll come onto at the end, as to why it's important to
see what happened with those, because the one thing
that's really obviously clear is that once this contract
was terminated, there ought to have been a final
accounting and reckoning between us at least,
irrespective of when the payment might come, to sort out
what our due entitlements were.
From, you know, January 2018 or February 2018 to
date, nothing has been assessed by the main contractor
on its termination of contract in respect of our, as it
were, what I might call our final account, which
includes our payment for entitlements, our payment for
variations, and what's happened with our EOT claims and
our prolongation claims and our loss of overhead
contribution claims and disruption claims, which were
put up to them for putting up the line on the basis that
they would be put up the line.
Where we sit here today is the respondent's case is,
quite simply: you don't get unless we get from the
employer, but without telling us what they've already
received or what they've done to put it up the line and
to chase it.
It is not us, if I may stress this, who are
particularly concerned about the main contract
proceedings.  We didn't start it, in a sense.  They
referred to the main contract proceedings as the first
and primary line of their defence, which is: there are
main contract proceedings, this tribunal shouldn't even
proceed with any claims because essentially we need to
know what the position is in the main contract
proceedings and you don't have any jurisdiction
beforehand.
I'm not going to travel over that old ground.  The
tribunal has made its award on that and we're here.
But the point is when you hear from me about the
main contract proceedings, I do not want you to think
that it's because I say that we are necessarily bound by
whatever is awarded up the line, but it is their duty to
tell us, if they're running a "pay if and when paid",
exactly what it is that they've put up the line and what
they've received from the employer and then to account
to us, because they have obligations in respect of that.
MR HARDING:  Mr Hickey, can I just ask you a question about
that.
I don't want to express any particular views, but on
the assumption that it would be proper for us to make
inferences of fact from the absence of information about
the main contract proceedings, what do you say those
inferences should be?  Because I'm concerned that it
would be very difficult for us to say: because there's a
lack of information, all your claims must be entirely
correct and payable.
MR HICKEY:  I don't put it as high as that, obviously.  I'm
loath to give a definitive answer to that.
MR HARDING:  You don't have to now, but it's a concern.
MR HICKEY:  I appreciate that.
Fortunately, back in England, they had a solution to
this problem which is if you don't challenge the
